short.label: About 50 words
short.text: Margaya is an open-source project management platform for teams that want clear ownership without heavy process. Plan work on boards, lists, spreadsheets, calendars and Gantt charts, write docs beside the tasks, and connect your tools through a REST API and MCP. Run it on your own server, free and open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0.

long.label: About 150 words
long.text: Margaya is an open-source project management platform built for teams that want to plan and ship work without the tool becoming a job of its own. Tasks move through board, list, spreadsheet, calendar and Gantt views of the same data. Cycles, modules, estimates and an intake inbox are there when a team needs planning, and stay out of the way when it doesn't. Teams write docs together next to their tasks, collect requests on public boards, and follow progress with analytics and an audit log. A REST API with an OpenAPI description, webhooks, an MCP server and integrations with GitHub, Gitea, Slack, Discord and others connect Margaya to the rest of a team's tools. The interface is available in 20 languages. Margaya is released under the GNU AGPL-3.0, with a commercial licence for use without its conditions, and runs on a single server with Docker, or on Kubernetes with Helm.

viewSpreadsheet.caption: Every property is a cell you can edit in place.

viewCalendar.caption: Drag a task to another day to reschedule it, then zoom in on the week.

The end of the first bar is dragged two days later, so it now ends after the blocked task starts: the line turns red and the task list flags the conflict.

palette.description: Demo: with a task open in the side sheet, Ctrl K opens the command bar. Typing “> status” narrows it to actions and shows “Change status…” for this task. Enter opens the status picker, the down arrow moves to In progress, and Enter applies it. A toast confirms “Status changed”.

cycles.caption: Cycles show progress as it happens: finish a task and the burn-down moves.

Its tasks are listed by status beside the cycle sidebar, which shows 55% progress, 16 of 30 points and a burn-down chart that draws itself against the ideal line. The cursor opens the status of “Cache avatar images” and picks Done. The task joins the Done group, progress rises to 64% and the chart drops to 4 tasks left.

estimates.caption: Estimates appear as chips on tasks and add up in cycles and modules.

selfHost.question: Can I host Margaya myself?
selfHost.answer: Yes. Run it with Docker Compose on a single server, or on Kubernetes with the official Helm chart. You need one app container and a PostgreSQL database. The install guide covers environment variables, storage and reverse proxies.

redis.question: Do I need Redis or other extra services?
redis.answer: No. A single server works without Redis. Redis is optional and only needed when you run several API instances and want realtime updates to reach every one of them.

data.question: Who owns my data?
data.answer: You do. Margaya runs only on your own server, so nothing leaves your infrastructure and we receive no data from it. You can export tasks to CSV, Excel or JSON at any time.

license.question: What licence is Margaya under?
license.answer: The GNU AGPL-3.0. You can use, change and host Margaya for free. If you modify it and let people use it over a network, you publish your changes under the same licence. To use Margaya without those conditions, for example to keep your changes private or build it into a closed product, you can get a commercial licence. Single sign-on, the audit log, the API and MCP are all in the open-source build.

cost.question: What does it cost?
cost.answer: Self-hosting Margaya under the AGPL-3.0 is free, with every feature included. Businesses that need to use it without the AGPL's conditions, such as keeping their changes private, can buy a commercial licence.

languages.question: Which languages does the app support?
languages.answer: The interface is available in 20 languages, and each person can choose their own.

jira.question: Can I move my work over from Jira?
jira.answer: Yes. Import the CSV file Jira exports, then map its statuses, priorities and people to your project. Margaya never connects to your Jira site, so no Jira token is needed. A generic CSV import covers other tools.

api.question: Is there an API, and does it work with AI agents?
api.answer: Every instance has a REST API described with OpenAPI, plus API keys and outgoing webhooks. A built-in MCP endpoint lets AI agents read and update tasks as the person who approved them.

ai.question: Does Margaya have AI, and is it on by default?
ai.answer: Yes, and no. Ask AI, Build mode, writing help, triage suggestions and AI agents are built in, but they stay off until an instance admin connects a model and a workspace turns AI on. Every change the AI proposes is shown to you first and can be undone.

aiData.question: Which AI models can I use, and where does my data go?
aiData.answer: Use Claude, or any OpenAI-compatible model you run yourself, such as Ollama or vLLM. With local-only routing nothing leaves your network. Margaya only sends what the person asking can already see, keeps no prompts or answers unless you turn on server history, and records usage counts for budgets.

jira.body: Upload Jira's CSV export, map statuses, priorities and people, and bring over sub-tasks, links and comments.

cleanup.title: Automation rules
cleanup.body: Set up When, If, Then rules for routine work, such as assigning or labelling new tasks, and archive or close stale tasks on a schedule, with a preview of what each rule will touch.

cta.title: Make Margaya part of your stack.
cta.description: Read the API reference, or connect your first integration in minutes.

ai.metaTitle: AI assistant, Build mode and agents
ai.metaDescription: Ask questions about your work and get answers from live data, let Build mode propose changes you confirm, write with AI help and assign tasks to AI agents, with your own model and AI off by default.
ai.title: An assistant that knows the work.
ai.description: Ask AI, Build mode, writing help and agents, all in the open-source build, running on the model you choose.

ask.title: Ask AI
ask.body: Ask in plain words and get answers from live tasks, with counts, charts and links to the tasks and pages it used. Mention a task, page or person with @, attach a file, or speak instead of typing.

build.title: Build mode
build.body: Describe a change, such as a project with three tasks or a task for Mia. You see what it read and how it reasoned, edit the proposed changes, confirm them, and undo any of them for an hour.

writing.title: Writing help
writing.body: Improve, shorten, translate or change the tone of a description or comment, get a title suggestion, summarise a task, or add an AI block to a page.

triage.title: Triage and briefs
triage.body: Get label and priority suggestions for new work, spot duplicates, filter a board by describing what you want, and get a summary of your unread inbox or a brief for a cycle.

agents.title: AI agents
agents.body: Agents are members you can assign tasks to. They ask a person when stuck, wait for approval before writing, run on a schedule, and can use tools from other MCP servers you connect.

privacy.title: Your model, your rules
privacy.body: AI is off until an admin turns it on. Use Claude or a local model, keep data on your network, set budgets, and keep no prompts or answers unless you choose to.

cta.title: Turn on AI when you are ready.
cta.description: Read the AI setup guide, or try Ask AI in a workspace of your own.

selfHost.metaTitle: Self-host Margaya with Docker or Helm
selfHost.metaDescription: Run Margaya on your own server with Docker Compose or Kubernetes with Helm. PostgreSQL only, Redis optional, AGPL-3.0 licensed, with trash, audit log and full exports.
selfHost.title: Run it yourself, keep everything.
selfHost.description: One app container and PostgreSQL. Every feature included, no feature gates, and nothing sent back to us.

deploy.title: Docker Compose or Helm
deploy.body: Start with Docker Compose on a single server, or deploy the official Helm chart to Kubernetes.

scale.title: Single server first, Redis when you scale
scale.body: One instance needs nothing but PostgreSQL. Add Redis only when several API instances must share realtime updates.

safety.title: Trash and audit log
safety.body: Deleted work waits in the trash for 30 days, and the audit log records who changed members, roles, keys and settings.

ownership.title: Your data, in open formats
ownership.body: Export tasks to CSV, Excel or JSON, sign in with your own OIDC provider, and keep backups wherever you like.

cta.title: Have it running in minutes.
cta.description: Follow the install guide and run Margaya on your own server.

firstLaunch.title: Install and first launch
firstLaunch.description: Your system asks once before it opens an app from the internet. After that, Margaya starts like any other app.

macos.step1: Open the downloaded .dmg and drag Margaya into Applications.
macos.step2: Open Margaya from Applications. When macOS asks about an app from the internet, click Open.
macos.step3: If macOS says it can't check the app, open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway.
macos.note: Start Margaya from Applications, not from the disk image, so links from your browser can open it.

windows.step2: If Windows shows "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway. The installer isn't code-signed yet.
windows.step3: Follow the installer. Margaya opens when it's done and appears in the Start menu.
windows.note: Updates install from inside the app and don't show this warning again.

linux.intro: Use the AppImage on any distribution, or install the package for yours. Run the commands in the folder you downloaded to.
linux.note: Margaya keeps your sign-in in the system keyring, so GNOME Keyring or KWallet must be running. To update a .deb or .rpm, install the next version's package.
